title: Why an Audience Helps and Hurts
text:
For decades, research on performing in front of others had been a puzzle. Some studies found that people and animals did better with an audience or alongside others: ants dug more, chickens ate more, people worked faster. Other studies found that an audience made people learn more slowly and make more mistakes.

In a short paper in Science in 1965, Robert Zajonc of the University of Michigan proposed a simple way to reconcile them. The presence of others, he argued, raises arousal, and arousal makes a creature more likely to do whatever response comes most naturally to it. On a well practiced or simple task, the natural response is the right one, so performance improves. On a new or complex task, the dominant response is often wrong, so performance gets worse.

Zajonc and his colleagues later tested the idea with cockroaches. Roaches ran a straight runway faster when other roaches watched from little boxes beside it, but took longer to solve a maze with a turn in it when watched. Studies with people found a similar pattern, for example good pool players shooting better and weak players shooting worse when observers stood nearby.
lesson: An audience magnifies what you already know. Rehearse new skills in private until they are habit, then perform them in front of the team.
